Set Shot count: 6 and Duration: 15s (Aspect ratio: 16:9) to structure a Seedance 2.0 commercial into six timed shots.

Lock the cast by explicitly stating CAST LOCK — exactly 3 people for the entire video and add “Never introduce any other person / no background people / no duplicates / every hand belongs only to these 3” to prevent extra characters and limb duplication.

Force a consistent period look by adding “apply to the FULL FRAME for the entire video” and then specifying a detailed film texture package (grain, halation, dust/scratches, gate weave, flicker, vignette, scanlines) for the target era.

Keep faces/product readable while aging the image by adding a constraint like “Clearly aged … but faces and the product stay readable.”

Prevent unwanted on-screen text by adding a strict text constraint: the ONLY text allowed is the final end card, plus “NO SUBTITLES / NO OTHER TEXT / NO CAPTIONS / NO WATERMARKS / NO UI ELEMENTS.”

Control narration placement by specifying “Narrator (final shot only)” and limiting dialogue to exact Japanese lines (e.g., Mother: 「おやすみなさい。」; Narrator: 「夏の夜に、夕凪香。」) with “Only the Japanese lines specified above; no other narration.”

Get era-accurate audio by adding “VINTAGE AUDIO TEXTURE — apply to ALL sound” and specifying mono, band-limited, hiss, wow/flutter, and “no modern stereo width / no crisp digital clarity.”

Maintain period correctness by listing explicit “no modern objects” constraints (e.g., no color TV/flat screens/plastic goods/modern clothing) alongside a detailed props/setting list.

Improve temporal consistency by stating “CHARACTERS & SETTING — identical in every shot” and then enumerating fixed wardrobe, props, and location details.

Reduce camera randomness by specifying per-shot camera instructions (fixed macro, slow tilt up, slow lateral dolly, slow push-in, slow pull-out) with exact timestamps for each shot segment.

For a 1950s look, explicitly prompt “entirely BLACK AND WHITE” and “vintage 35mm monochrome film” plus high-contrast B&W texture settings to avoid any color tint.

Avoid common generation artifacts by adding an “Avoid:” block (extra hands/limbs, deformation, character drift, robotic voice, modern digital-clean look, modern music, garbled/misspelled logo text).

--- THREAD CONTINUATION ---
[Thread 1] 1960s prompt ↓
--------------
Shot count: 6 | Duration: 15s | Aspect ratio: 16:9
A live-action Japanese TV commercial for a mosquito coil, filmed in the late
1960s (Showa 40s era) — shot on early vintage color film and looking like a
genuine surviving commercial print from that time.
VINTAGE COLOR FILM TEXTURE — apply to the FULL FRAME for the entire video:
1960s color film stock look — strongly faded colors with the classic aged
Eastmancolor shift (magenta-leaning cast, washed-out cyans, creamy whites),
noticeable film grain, glowing halation around the ember, light bulbs and
highlights, frequent small dust specks and hairline scratches drifting frame
to frame, gentle gate weave (slow frame wobble), occasional brightness flicker,
soft vintage lens focus with gentle vignette, and faint CRT scanlines
underneath, as if replayed from an old broadcast recording.
Clearly aged — older and rougher than a 1970s print — but faces and the product
stay readable.
CAST LOCK — the cast is EXACTLY 3 people for the entire video:
father, mother, one little girl. Never introduce any other person in any shot:
no neighbors, no background people, no duplicates. Every hand on screen belongs
only to these 3 people.
CHARACTERS & SETTING — identical in every shot, authentic Showa 40s (late 1960s)
Japan:
- Father: white tank-top undershirt (running shirt), short neat hair, calm
  gentle face, paper uchiwa fan.
- Mother: white kappogi apron over a simple summer dress, hair tied back,
  soft kind expression.
- Little girl: about 5 years old, bob haircut, light cotton summer pajamas.
- Product: "Yunagiko" mosquito coil — a classic deep-green spiral coil resting
  on a ceramic pig-shaped burner (kayaributa). No readable text on the product.
- Setting: a modest wooden Japanese house on a summer evening, late 1960s —
  a tatami living room with a round chabudai low table, a small black-and-white
  TV with a rounded screen glowing softly, an electric fan with metal blades
  slowly oscillating, wooden-frame windows and engawa veranda open to a small
  garden, sudare blinds, wind chime, a hanging mosquito net over the child's
  futon, watermelon on the table. Everything period-correct for the late 1960s:
  no color TV, no modern flat screens, no plastic goods, no contemporary objects.
VOICES — 1970s Japanese TV commercial style:
- Mother: one soft, tender line, natural and quiet.
- Narrator (final shot only): deep, warm male announcer in classic 1960s
  Japanese commercial style — measured, formal, slightly grand delivery,
  unhurried, with rounded old-broadcast enunciation.
VINTAGE AUDIO TEXTURE — apply to ALL sound for the entire video:
warm analog mono sound as if from a 1970s TV broadcast — narrow band-limited
frequency range, gentle tape saturation and soft hiss, slight wow and flutter,
no modern stereo width, no crisp digital clarity.
STYLE:
authentic late-1960s Japanese commercial cinematography — warm tungsten interior
light against deep blue evening outside the window, stately fixed compositions,
slow deliberate camera moves, cinematic smoke drifting through lamplight, quiet
poetic pacing, documentary realism of everyday high-growth-era Showa family life.
FOCUS:
the beauty of curling smoke in warm lamplight, the glowing orange coil ember
against the deep-green spiral, tactile period detail (ceramic pig burner,
mosquito net, tank-top father with uchiwa, humming electric fan), the family's
quiet peaceful expressions, consistent aged color-film texture.
[0s – 2s]
SHOT 1 — HOOK: THE MATCH.
Dim evening interior. Extreme macro of a hand striking a match — the flame
flares with warm halation, lighting the fingertips orange against the dusk.
The sharp strike and hiss of the match head igniting.
Camera: fixed macro.
[2s – 4s]
SHOT 2 — LIGHTING THE COIL.
Macro: the match flame touches the tip of the deep-green spiral coil; the ember
catches with an orange glow, and the first thin thread of smoke rises through
the warm light.
Camera: fixed macro.
[4s – 6.5s]
SHOT 3 — SMOKE IN THE LAMPLIGHT.
The ceramic pig burner sits by the open window; smoke curls upward through the
warm glow of the room lamp, swaying gently as the electric fan hums and the
wind chime rings once. Deep blue dusk outside the insect screen.
Camera: slow tilt up, following the smoke.
[6.5s – 9s]
SHOT 4 — SUMMER EVENING AT HOME.
The family relaxes in the tatami living room: the father in his tank top slowly
waving his uchiwa, the mother and the little girl sharing watermelon by the low
table, the small black-and-white TV glowing softly, thin smoke drifting across the
foreground.
Camera: slow lateral dolly.
[9s – 12s]
SHOT 5 — UNDER THE MOSQUITO NET.
The little girl sleeps peacefully under the hanging mosquito net; the mother
kneels beside it, gazing at her gently, then smiles softly.
Mother (whispering, tender, Japanese): 「おやすみなさい。」
Camera: slow push-in.
[12s – 15s]
SHOT 6 — PRODUCT FINALE WITH END CARD.
Night stillness: the pig burner and the glowing coil in the foreground, a single
line of smoke rising, the quiet dim room behind. In the last 1.5 seconds,
a retro end card appears centered on screen:
Text: 「夕凪香」 — bold hand-painted 1960s Japanese gothic lettering with
slightly uneven hand-drawn edges, warm white with a thin dark outline,
simply fading in, like a hand-lettered vintage commercial end card.
Keep the text large, correct, and clearly readable.
Narrator (deep warm 1960s announcer, Japanese): 「夏の夜に、夕凪香。」
Camera: slow pull-out.
MUSIC — gentle 1960s Japanese commercial score for a quiet night mood:
soft electric organ and vibraphone with a hint of accordion, simple and
old-fashioned, and a small female chorus humming warmly in the final two shots
(wordless humming only, no lyrics). Mono, tape-warm, slightly warped with
audible age. The music stays under the ambience and blooms gently for the
end card.
Additional sounds: the match strike, the faint crackle of the ember, the low hum
of the electric fan, higurashi cicadas and night insects outside, wind chime,
a bite of watermelon

Bloquea el reparto indicando explícitamente CAST LOCK — exactamente 3 personas durante todo el video y añade “Never introduce any other person / no background people / no duplicates / every hand belongs only to these 3” para evitar personajes extra y duplicación de extremidades.

Fuerza un look de época consistente añadiendo “apply to the FULL FRAME for the entire video” y luego especificando un paquete detallado de textura fílmica (grain, halation, dust/scratches, gate weave, flicker, vignette, scanlines) para la era objetivo.

Mantén los rostros/producto legibles mientras envejeces la imagen añadiendo una restricción como “Clearly aged … but faces and the product stay readable.”

Evita texto no deseado en pantalla con una restricción estricta: el ÚNICO texto permitido es la tarjeta final de cierre, además de “NO SUBTITLES / NO OTHER TEXT / NO CAPTIONS / NO WATERMARKS / NO UI ELEMENTS.”

Controla la ubicación de la narración especificando “Narrator (final shot only)” y limitando el diálogo a líneas exactas en japonés (por ejemplo, Mother: 「おやすみなさい。」; Narrator: 「夏の夜に、夕凪香。」) con “Only the Japanese lines specified above; no other narration.”

Consigue audio fiel a la época añadiendo “VINTAGE AUDIO TEXTURE — apply to ALL sound” y especificando mono, band-limited, hiss, wow/flutter, y “no modern stereo width / no crisp digital clarity.”

Mantén la corrección histórica enumerando restricciones explícitas de “no modern objects” (por ejemplo, no color TV/flat screens/plastic goods/modern clothing) junto con una lista detallada de props/setting.

Mejora la consistencia temporal indicando “CHARACTERS & SETTING — identical in every shot” y luego enumerando vestuario, props y detalles de la ubicación fijos.

Reduce la aleatoriedad de cámara especificando instrucciones por toma (fixed macro, slow tilt up, slow lateral dolly, slow push-in, slow pull-out) con timestamps exactos para cada segmento.

Para un look de los 1950s, indica explícitamente “entirely BLACK AND WHITE” y “vintage 35mm monochrome film” más ajustes de textura B&W de alto contraste para evitar cualquier tinte de color.

Evita artefactos comunes de generación añadiendo un bloque “Avoid:” (extra hands/limbs, deformation, character drift, robotic voice, modern digital-clean look, modern music, garbled or misspelled logo text).

Vous êtes un traducteur professionnel spécialisé dans les contenus liés à l’IA et aux technologies créatives.

Traduisez le texte suivant en français.

Règles :
1. Conservez avec précision tous les termes techniques (par ex. « prompt », « cinématique », « camera pan » peuvent rester en anglais ou être traduits par les équivalents établis dans la langue cible).
2. Gardez un ton naturel et fluide dans la langue cible — pas une traduction mot à mot.
3. Préservez tout le formatage (retours à la ligne, puces).
4. Si le texte contient un véritable prompt Seedance/IA (instructions de génération), laissez-le en anglais et traduisez uniquement le contexte/l’explication autour.

Texte à traduire :
---
Définissez Shot count : 6 et Duration : 15s (Aspect ratio : 16:9) pour structurer un spot Seedance 2.0 en six plans minutés.

Verrouillez le casting en indiquant explicitement CAST LOCK — exactement 3 personnes pour toute la vidéo — et ajoutez « Never introduce any other person / no background people / no duplicates / every hand belongs only to these 3 » afin d’éviter les personnages supplémentaires et la duplication des membres.

Imposez un rendu d’époque cohérent en ajoutant « apply to the FULL FRAME for the entire video » puis en précisant un package détaillé de texture film (grain, halation, dust/scratches, gate weave, flicker, vignette, scanlines) pour l’époque visée.

Gardez les visages/le produit lisibles tout en vieillissant l’image en ajoutant une contrainte du type « Clearly aged … but faces and the product stay readable. »

Empêchez les textes indésirables à l’écran en ajoutant une contrainte stricte sur le texte : le SEUL texte autorisé est la carte de fin finale, plus « NO SUBTITLES / NO OTHER TEXT / NO CAPTIONS / NO WATERMARKS / NO UI ELEMENTS. »

Contrôlez le placement de la narration en précisant « Narrator (final shot only) » et en limitant les dialogues à des répliques japonaises exactes (par ex. Mother: 「おやすみなさい。」; Narrator: 「夏の夜に、夕凪香。」) avec « Only the Japanese lines specified above; no other narration. »

Obtenez un audio fidèle à l’époque en ajoutant « VINTAGE AUDIO TEXTURE — apply to ALL sound » et en précisant mono, band-limited, hiss, wow/flutter, et « no modern stereo width / no crisp digital clarity. »

Maintenez l’exactitude historique en listant des contraintes explicites « no modern objects » (par ex. pas de color TV/flat screens/plastic goods/modern clothing) en parallèle d’une liste détaillée d’accessoires/décor.

Améliorez la cohérence temporelle en indiquant « CHARACTERS & SETTING — identical in every shot » puis en énumérant les costumes, accessoires et détails de lieu fixes.

Réduisez l’aléatoire de la caméra en précisant des instructions caméra plan par plan (fixed macro, slow tilt up, slow lateral dolly, slow push-in, slow pull-out) avec des timestamps exacts pour chaque segment.

Pour un rendu des années 1950, demandez explicitement « entirely BLACK AND WHITE » et « vintage 35mm monochrome film » ainsi que des réglages de texture B&W à fort contraste afin d’éviter toute dominante colorée.

Évitez les artefacts de génération courants en ajoutant un bloc « Avoid: » (mains/membres supplémentaires, déformation, character drift, robotic voice, modern digital-clean look, modern music, garbled or misspelled logo text).
